source.excerpt: Source prompt: What induces the formation of the neural plate from ectoderm? Source answer: Appearance of the notochord and prechordal mesoderm induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate. The induced cells form neuroectoderm.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which process is most accurately described as neurulation?

options.text: Epithelial organization of a mesodermal ball followed by formation of somite components
Morphologic transformation of the neural plate into the neural tube through neural-fold elevation, neural-groove formation, and closure
Delamination and migration of crest cells into the underlying mesoderm
Temporary connection of paraxial mesoderm to lateral plate mesoderm

acceptedFreeText: Morphologic transformation of the neural plate into the neural tube through neural-fold elevation, neural-groove formation, and closure
questions.explanation: Neurulation is the morphologic transformation of the neural plate into the neural tube. It includes convergent extension, formation and elevation of the neural folds, development of the neural groove, and neural-tube closure with transient cranial and caudal neuropores.

distractorExplanations.A: This describes early somite transformation rather than neurulation.
distractorExplanations.B: Correct. These coordinated morphologic changes convert the neural plate into the neural tube.
distractorExplanations.C: This describes epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migration of neural crest cells, not the entire process of neurulation.
distractorExplanations.D: This describes the temporary relationship of intermediate mesoderm to adjacent mesodermal regions.

questions.learningObjective: Define neurulation by its principal morphologic events.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Define neurulation. Source answer: Neurulation is the process by which the neural plate morphologically transforms into the neural tube. It involves convergent extension, formation and elevation of neural folds, development of the neural groove, and closure of the neural tube, leaving transient cranial and caudal neuropores.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly orders the major morphologic events of neural-tube formation?

options.text: Neural-fold fusion → neural-plate lengthening → neural-groove formation → neuropore closure
Neural-groove formation → neural-plate lengthening → neural-fold elevation → midline fusion
Neuropore closure → neural-fold elevation → neural-plate lengthening → midline fusion
Neural-plate lengthening → neural-fold elevation and neural-groove formation → midline fusion → temporary neuropores followed by closure

acceptedFreeText: Neural-plate lengthening → neural-fold elevation and neural-groove formation → midline fusion → temporary neuropores followed by closure
questions.explanation: The neural plate first lengthens through convergent extension. Its lateral edges elevate as neural folds while the midline becomes the neural groove. The folds then approach and fuse in the midline, leaving temporary anterior and posterior neuropores that communicate with the amniotic cavity until closure.

distractorExplanations.A: Fusion cannot precede neural-plate lengthening and formation of the folds and groove.
distractorExplanations.B: Neural-plate lengthening precedes development of the neural groove and elevation of the folds.
distractorExplanations.C: Neuropore closure is a late event rather than the first step in neural-tube formation.
distractorExplanations.D: Correct. This sequence follows neural-plate remodeling through fold fusion and eventual neuropore closure.

questions.learningObjective: Sequence the principal morphologic steps of neural-tube formation.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Describe the key morphological steps of neural tube formation from the neural plate. Source answer: 1) Neural plate lengthens (with convergent extension). 2) Lateral edges elevate to form neural folds. 3) Midline region becomes the neural groove. 4) Neural folds approach each other and fuse in the midline (starting at cervical region, then moving cranially and caudally). 5) Temporary anterior and posterior neuropores communicate with the amniotic cavity until they close.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: During neural-tube closure, cells at the lateral border of the neuroectoderm lose their epithelial organization. What is their subsequent fate?

options.text: They undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, delaminate, and migrate into the underlying mesoderm as neural crest cells.
They remain epithelial and form the midline neural groove.
They become intermediate mesoderm connecting paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm.
They form ventromedial somite cells that surround the notochord.

acceptedFreeText: They undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, delaminate, and migrate into the underlying mesoderm as neural crest cells.
questions.explanation: Cells at the crest or lateral border of the neuroectoderm undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. They then delaminate and migrate into the underlying mesoderm as neural crest cells.

distractorExplanations.A: Correct. Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, delamination, and migration establish the neural crest cell population.
distractorExplanations.B: These crest cells lose, rather than retain, epithelial organization and migrate away from the neural folds.
distractorExplanations.C: Intermediate mesoderm is a mesodermal region and is not formed by these crest neuroectodermal cells.
distractorExplanations.D: Ventromedial somite cells form sclerotome; they are not the cells delaminating from the neural-fold crest.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the cellular origin and emergence of neural crest cells during neural-tube closure.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What happens to ectodermal cells at the crest of the neural folds during neural tube closure? Source answer: Cells at the lateral border/crest of the neuroectoderm undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), delaminate, and migrate into the underlying mesoderm as neural crest cells (NCCs).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: An experimental intervention neutralizes noggin, chordin, and follistatin released by the organizer. Which immediate developmental mechanism is most directly disrupted?

options.text: Migration of ventrolateral somite cells into parietal lateral plate mesoderm
Temporary connection of paraxial mesoderm with lateral plate mesoderm
Inhibition of BMP in cranial mesoderm that permits dorsalized mesoderm formation and contributes to neural induction
Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition of cells at the neural-fold crest

acceptedFreeText: Inhibition of BMP in cranial mesoderm that permits dorsalized mesoderm formation and contributes to neural induction
questions.explanation: Noggin, chordin, and follistatin are secreted by the organizer and inhibit BMP in cranial mesoderm. This permits formation of the notochord and paraxial, or dorsalized, mesoderm and contributes to neural induction.

distractorExplanations.A: This is a step in somite-derived muscle-cell migration, not the stated action of organizer-derived BMP inhibitors.
distractorExplanations.B: This describes the position of intermediate mesoderm, not the mechanism mediated by noggin, chordin, and follistatin.
distractorExplanations.C: Correct. Neutralizing these organizer factors would directly remove their inhibition of BMP in cranial mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.D: This describes neural crest formation rather than the specified BMP-inhibitory mechanism in cranial mesoderm.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how organizer-derived BMP inhibitors support dorsalization and cranial neural induction.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Which molecules from the organizer inhibit BMP to allow dorsalization and neural induction in the cranial region? Source answer: Noggin, chordin, and follistatin are secreted by the organizer (node). They inhibit BMP expression in cranial mesoderm, allowing formation of notochord and paraxial (dorsalized) mesoderm and contributing to neural induction.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A mesodermal region lies temporarily between paraxial mesoderm and lateral plate mesoderm. Which description correctly identifies this region and its later derivatives?

options.text: Paraxial mesoderm; it forms kidneys, gonads, and their ducts.
Intermediate mesoderm; it forms kidneys, gonads, and their ducts.
Lateral plate mesoderm; it forms vertebrae, ribs, and dermis of the back.
Sclerotome; it forms cranial nerve and dorsal root ganglia.

acceptedFreeText: Intermediate mesoderm; it forms kidneys, gonads, and their ducts.
questions.explanation: Intermediate mesoderm temporarily connects paraxial mesoderm with lateral plate mesoderm. It later differentiates into urogenital structures, including the kidneys, gonads, and their ducts.

distractorExplanations.A: The connecting region is intermediate, not paraxial, mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.B: Correct. Both the temporary anatomic relationship and the urogenital derivatives identify intermediate mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.C: The connecting region is not lateral plate mesoderm, and vertebrae, ribs, and back dermis are somite derivatives.
distractorExplanations.D: Sclerotome is a somite component and does not form the listed neural crest-derived ganglia.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the position and major derivatives of intermediate mesoderm.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is intermediate mesoderm and what does it connect? Source answer: Intermediate mesoderm is a region of mesoderm that temporarily connects paraxial mesoderm with lateral plate mesoderm. It later differentiates into urogenital structures (kidneys, gonads, and their ducts).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Full BMP activity is maintained during gastrulation. Which combination of ectodermal and mesodermal fates is expected?

options.text: Neuroectoderm with notochord and paraxial mesoderm
Epidermis with notochord and paraxial mesoderm
Neuroectoderm with intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm
Epidermis with intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm

acceptedFreeText: Epidermis with intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm
questions.explanation: In the presence of BMP, ectoderm adopts an epidermal rather than neural fate, while mesoderm becomes ventralized into intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm.

distractorExplanations.A: Neuroectoderm and dorsalized mesoderm are not the fates produced by full BMP activity.
distractorExplanations.B: The epidermal fate is consistent with BMP, but notochord and paraxial mesoderm are dorsalized rather than BMP-driven ventral mesodermal fates.
distractorExplanations.C: Intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm are consistent with BMP activity, but the accompanying ectodermal fate should be epidermis rather than neuroectoderm.
distractorExplanations.D: Correct. Full BMP activity drives epidermal ectoderm and ventralized intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm.

questions.learningObjective: Predict ectodermal and mesodermal fates produced by BMP signaling during gastrulation.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What does BMP signaling normally do to ectoderm and mesoderm in the gastrulating embryo? Source answer: In the presence of BMP (bone morphogenetic proteins): • Ectoderm → epidermis • Mesoderm → intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm (ventralization). So full BMP activity drives non-neural ectoderm and ventral mesoderm fates.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: During examination of an embryo undergoing neurulation, the first point of neural-fold fusion is identified. Where should it be located, and how should fusion proceed from that point?

options.text: In the cervical region near the fifth somite, proceeding cranially and caudally
At the cranial neuropore, proceeding only caudally
At the caudal neuropore, proceeding only cranially
Along the entire neural plate simultaneously

acceptedFreeText: In the cervical region near the fifth somite, proceeding cranially and caudally
questions.explanation: Neural-tube fusion begins in the cervical region around the level of the fifth somite. Fusion then proceeds in both cranial and caudal directions.

distractorExplanations.A: Correct. The cervical region near the fifth somite is the initiation site, followed by bidirectional progression.
distractorExplanations.B: Fusion does not begin at the cranial neuropore and is not described as progressing only caudally.
distractorExplanations.C: Fusion does not begin at the caudal neuropore and is not described as progressing only cranially.
distractorExplanations.D: Neural-tube fusion begins at a defined cervical site rather than occurring simultaneously along the entire plate.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the initiation site and direction of neural-tube fusion.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Where and when does neural tube fusion begin? Source answer: Neural tube fusion begins in the cervical region around the level of the fifth somite and then proceeds cranially and caudally.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A population of ventromedial cells in an epithelialized somite loses epithelial organization and becomes mesenchymal. What does this population form, and where does it migrate?

options.text: Dermatome; it remains dorsally and later forms dermis of the back.
Myotome; it migrates into parietal lateral plate mesoderm to form all segmental structures.
Sclerotome; it migrates around the neural tube and notochord.
Neural crest; it delaminates from the neural folds and migrates into the somite lumen.

acceptedFreeText: Sclerotome; it migrates around the neural tube and notochord.
questions.explanation: Ventromedial somite cells lose their epithelial organization, become mesenchymal, and migrate around the neural tube and notochord. This population is the sclerotome, which will contribute to vertebrae and ribs.

distractorExplanations.A: Remaining dorsal somite cells form dermatome, but the ventromedial cells described form sclerotome.
distractorExplanations.B: Muscle precursors arise at dorsomedial and ventrolateral edges; only some ventrolateral cells migrate into parietal lateral plate mesoderm to form body-wall and limb muscles.
distractorExplanations.C: Correct. Mesenchymal ventromedial somite cells become sclerotome and surround the neural tube and notochord.
distractorExplanations.D: Neural crest cells arise from the lateral border of neuroectoderm, not from ventromedial somite cells.

questions.learningObjective: Relate early somite cell position and morphologic change to formation of the sclerotome.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Describe the early morphologic transformation of a somite into its main components. Source answer: 1) Somite initially forms as a ball of mesoderm that epithelizes, creating a donut-shaped structure around a small lumen. 2) Ventromedial cells lose epithelial organization, become mesenchymal, and migrate around neural tube and notochord → sclerotome (future vertebrae and ribs). 3) Cells at dorsomedial and ventrolateral edges become muscle precursors; remaining dorsal cells form dermatome. 4) Muscle precursors become mesenchymal and migrate beneath dermatome → dermomyotome; some ventrolateral cells migrate into parietal lateral plate to form body wall and limb muscles. 5) Dermatome cells later become dermis of back.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which option correctly matches all three principal somite components with their derivatives?

options.text: Sclerotome—skeletal muscle; myotome—dermis of the back; dermatome—vertebrae and ribs
Sclerotome—vertebrae, ribs, tendons, and cartilage; myotome—skeletal muscle; dermatome—dermis of the back
Sclerotome—dermis of the back; myotome—vertebrae and ribs; dermatome—skeletal muscle
Sclerotome—urogenital structures; myotome—cranial nerve ganglia; dermatome—epidermis

acceptedFreeText: Sclerotome—vertebrae, ribs, tendons, and cartilage; myotome—skeletal muscle; dermatome—dermis of the back
questions.explanation: Each somite produces sclerotome, myotome, and dermatome. Sclerotome forms vertebrae, ribs, tendons, and cartilage; myotome forms skeletal muscle; and dermatome forms dermis of the back. Myotome and dermatome retain their segmental nerve supply.

distractorExplanations.A: The derivatives are mismatched: skeletal muscle is myotomal, back dermis is dermatomal, and vertebrae and ribs are sclerotomal.
distractorExplanations.B: Correct. Each somite component is paired with its proper derivative.
distractorExplanations.C: The three derivatives are assigned to the wrong somite components.
distractorExplanations.D: Urogenital structures arise from intermediate mesoderm, the listed ganglia are neural crest derivatives, and BMP-directed ectoderm forms epidermis; none is the stated component mapping.

questions.learningObjective: Match sclerotome, myotome, and dermatome with their major derivatives.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What tissues does each somite ultimately give rise to? Source answer: Each somite forms: • Sclerotome → vertebrae, ribs, tendons, and cartilage. • Myotome → skeletal muscle (segmental muscle component). • Dermatome → dermis of the back. Each retains segmental innervation (myotome and dermatome keep their segmental nerve supply).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Migrating neural crest cells become loosely organized embryonic connective tissue even though they originated from ectoderm. Which statement best distinguishes mesenchyme from mesoderm?

options.text: Mesenchyme and mesoderm are synonymous terms for the same germ-layer identity.
Mesenchyme is restricted to cells derived from mesoderm, whereas mesoderm may arise from any germ layer.
Mesoderm describes loose cellular organization, whereas mesenchyme describes epiblast origin.
Mesoderm denotes a germ-layer identity, whereas mesenchyme denotes loosely organized embryonic connective tissue regardless of germ-layer origin.

acceptedFreeText: Mesoderm denotes a germ-layer identity, whereas mesenchyme denotes loosely organized embryonic connective tissue regardless of germ-layer origin.
questions.explanation: Mesoderm is a germ-layer identity applied to cells derived from the epiblast and extraembryonic tissues. Mesenchyme describes loosely organized embryonic connective tissue and may have ectodermal, mesodermal, or endodermal origin.

distractorExplanations.A: The terms are not synonymous: one describes germ-layer identity and the other describes tissue organization.
distractorExplanations.B: Mesenchyme is not restricted to mesodermal origin; it may originate from ectoderm, mesoderm, or endoderm.
distractorExplanations.C: This reverses the definitions. Mesoderm is the germ-layer term, while mesenchyme describes loose embryonic connective tissue.
distractorExplanations.D: Correct. The distinction is germ-layer identity versus tissue organization independent of germ-layer origin.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate the germ-layer term mesoderm from the morphologic term mesenchyme.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Differentiate mesoderm from mesenchyme in this context. Source answer: Mesoderm: cells derived from the epiblast and extraembryonic tissues (germ layer identity). Mesenchyme: loosely organized embryonic connective tissue regardless of its germ layer origin (ectoderm, mesoderm, or endoderm).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which group consists entirely of neural crest cell derivatives?

options.text: Dorsal root ganglia, melanocytes, and adrenal medulla
Epidermis, dermis of the back, and conotruncal septum

acceptedFreeText: Dorsal root ganglia, melanocytes, and adrenal medulla
questions.explanation: Spinal dorsal root ganglia, melanocytes, and the adrenal medulla are all derivatives of neural crest cells.

distractorExplanations.A: Correct. Every structure in this group is a listed neural crest derivative.
distractorExplanations.B: Adrenal medulla is neural crest-derived, but kidneys and gonads are derivatives of intermediate mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.C: Melanocytes are neural crest-derived, but vertebrae and ribs arise from sclerotome.
distractorExplanations.D: The conotruncal septum is neural crest-derived, but epidermis is a BMP-directed ectodermal fate and dermis of the back arises from dermatome.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: List major derivatives of neural crest cells (NCCs). Source answer: Selected key derivatives: • Connective tissue and bones of face and skull • Cranial nerve ganglia • C cells (parafollicular cells) of thyroid • Conotruncal septum of the heart • Odontoblasts (dentin-forming cells) • Dermis of face and neck • Spinal (dorsal root) ganglia • Sympathetic chain and preaortic ganglia • Parasympathetic ganglia of GI tract • Adrenal medulla • Schwann and glial cells • Meninges (forebrain) • Melanocytes • Smooth muscle in blood vessels of face and forebrain

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What long-term adult diseases are associated with IUGR (Barker hypothesis)? Source answer: Higher risk of obesity, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes in adulthood.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.topic: Fetal period, placenta, and fetal membranes
questions.subtopic: Prenatal therapy for congenital adrenal hyperplasia
questions.prompt: A female fetus is affected by the usual form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Which combination of pathogenesis and prenatal management is correct?

options.text: Androgen deficiency with normal cortisol; maternal dexamethasone is given to increase virilization.
21-hydroxylase deficiency causing high cortisol and low androgen levels; maternal dexamethasone reduces adrenal hyperplasia.
21-hydroxylase deficiency causing low cortisol, adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen excess; maternal dexamethasone reduces virilization.
21-hydroxylase deficiency causing low cortisol and androgen excess; no prenatal maternal treatment is available.

acceptedFreeText: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causing low cortisol, adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen excess; maternal dexamethasone reduces virilization.
questions.explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is usually caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency, producing low cortisol, adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen excess. Prenatal maternal dexamethasone treatment reduces virilization of an affected female fetus.

distractorExplanations.A: The usual disorder involves androgen excess and low cortisol, and treatment is intended to reduce rather than increase virilization.
distractorExplanations.B: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes low cortisol and androgen excess, not high cortisol and low androgen levels; the stated prenatal goal is reduced virilization.
distractorExplanations.C: This correctly combines the usual cause, hormonal consequences, adrenal response, and prenatal treatment effect.
distractorExplanations.D: Although the stated deficiency, low cortisol, and androgen excess are consistent with the disorder, maternal dexamethasone can be used prenatally to reduce virilization.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the usual basis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and its prenatal treatment.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) and how can it be treated prenatally? Source answer: Usually due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency causing low cortisol, adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen excess. Prenatal maternal treatment with dexamethasone reduces virilization of affected female fetuses.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: During embryogenesis, coordinated changes in cell shape, size, position, number, and adhesivity cause an embryonic structure to acquire its characteristic three-dimensional form. Which process is being described?
questions.explanation: Morphogenesis is the form-shaping process through which the embryo and its parts acquire their characteristic three-dimensional shape and structure. It is driven by cell behaviors that generate differential growth.

distractorExplanations.A: Induction is signaling by an inducing tissue that changes the fate or behavior of a competent responding tissue; it is not the overall acquisition of three-dimensional form.
distractorExplanations.B: Differential growth is the unequal growth produced by the listed cell behaviors. It drives morphogenesis but is not the broader form-shaping process described.
distractorExplanations.C: Morphogenesis correctly names the acquisition of characteristic three-dimensional embryonic shape and structure through fundamental cell behaviors.
distractorExplanations.D: Dysmorphogenesis is abnormal morphogenesis caused by perturbation of differential growth, whereas the stem describes normal form generation.

questions.learningObjective: Define morphogenesis and relate it to the cell behaviors that shape the embryo.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is morphogenesis? Source answer: Morphogenesis is the form-shaping process in embryogenesis by which the embryo and its parts acquire their characteristic 3D shape and structure. It is driven by fundamental cell behaviors that generate differential growth (changes in cell shape, size, position, number, and adhesivity).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: One region of a simple embryonic primordium grows more rapidly than an adjacent region because of differences in cell shape, size, position, number, and adhesivity. Which mechanism most directly accounts for the resulting complex form?
questions.explanation: Differential growth is unequal growth of different embryonic parts driven by changes in cell behavior. It underlies morphogenesis and can transform relatively simple primordia into complex forms.

distractorExplanations.A: Differential growth is correct because the regions undergo unequal growth as a result of differing cell behaviors.
distractorExplanations.B: Fate mapping labels cells and tracks where they ultimately reside; it does not itself produce unequal regional growth.
distractorExplanations.C: Induction changes the fate or behavior of a competent responding tissue through signals from an inducing tissue, but the stem specifically emphasizes unequal growth.
distractorExplanations.D: Dysmorphogenesis is an abnormal perturbation of differential growth that produces structural birth defects; no abnormality is described here.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize differential growth as the mechanism by which unequal cell behaviors generate embryonic form.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is differential growth in embryology? Source answer: Differential growth is unequal growth of different parts of the embryo, driven by changes in cell behaviors (shape, size, position, number, adhesivity). It underlies morphogenesis and creates complex forms from relatively simple primordia.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Two permanent morphologic abnormalities are classified. The first resulted from a primary defect in formation of a structure; the second was imposed on an already-forming structure by mechanical forces. Which classification is correct?

options.text: Neither is a structural birth defect
Only the first is a structural birth defect
Both are structural birth defects; the first is a malformation and the second is a deformation

acceptedFreeText: Both are structural birth defects; the first is a malformation and the second is a deformation
questions.explanation: Structural birth defects are permanent morphologic abnormalities arising from dysmorphogenesis. A primary defect in formation is a malformation, whereas a secondary defect imposed by mechanical forces is a deformation.

distractorExplanations.A: Both abnormalities meet the definition of structural birth defects because both are permanent morphologic abnormalities.
distractorExplanations.B: Deformations as well as malformations are included among structural birth defects, so the second abnormality also qualifies.
distractorExplanations.C: Only the mechanically imposed secondary abnormality is a deformation; the primary formation defect is a malformation.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly classifies both abnormalities and distinguishes a primary malformation from a mechanically produced deformation.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish malformations from deformations within the category of structural birth defects.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are structural birth defects? Source answer: Structural birth defects are permanent, morphologic abnormalities of organs or body parts arising from dysmorphogenesis. They include: • Malformations (primary defects in formation of a structure) • Deformations (secondary defects due to mechanical forces).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A club foot develops when oligohydramnios mechanically constrains an already-forming structure. Which term most specifically classifies this defect?
questions.explanation: A deformation is a secondary morphologic defect imposed on an already-forming structure by extrinsic mechanical forces. Club foot caused by mechanical constraint in oligohydramnios is an example.

distractorExplanations.A: A malformation is a primary defect in formation, whereas this defect is secondary to an extrinsic mechanical force.
distractorExplanations.B: Deformation is correct because mechanical constraint secondarily alters an already-forming structure.
distractorExplanations.C: A syndrome is a pattern of multiple primary malformations with one underlying cause, not a single mechanically imposed defect.
distractorExplanations.D: Induction is a signaling interaction between an inducing tissue and a competent responding tissue, not a category of morphologic defect.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a deformation from its secondary mechanical mechanism.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Define deformation in embryology. Source answer: Deformation = a secondary morphologic defect imposed on an already-forming structure by extrinsic mechanical forces, indirectly affecting its development (e.g., club foot from mechanical constraint in oligohydramnios).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: An affected individual has multiple primary malformations that are all attributable to a single chromosomal cause. Which term best describes this pattern?
questions.explanation: A syndrome is a pattern of multiple primary malformations sharing a single underlying genetic, chromosomal, or environmental cause.

distractorExplanations.A: Differential growth is unequal growth of embryonic regions and is a mechanism underlying morphogenesis, not a diagnostic pattern of malformations.
distractorExplanations.B: A deformation is a secondary morphologic defect caused by an extrinsic mechanical force, not multiple primary malformations with one cause.
distractorExplanations.C: Syndrome is correct because the pattern consists of multiple primary malformations linked to a single underlying cause.
distractorExplanations.D: A fate map records where labeled embryonic cells ultimately reside; it does not classify a pattern of abnormalities.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the defining relationship between multiple primary malformations and a syndrome.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is a syndrome in embryology/clinical genetics? Source answer: A syndrome is a pattern of multiple primary malformations with a single underlying cause (genetic, chromosomal, or environmental). Examples include Down syndrome (trisomy 21) and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A genetic mutation and a teratogen disrupt the cell behaviors responsible for differential growth, producing a structural birth defect. Which process has occurred?
questions.explanation: Dysmorphogenesis is abnormal morphogenesis caused by perturbation of differential growth through genetic mutation, teratogen exposure, or both, resulting in structural birth defects.

distractorExplanations.A: Dysmorphogenesis is correct because genetic and environmental factors have perturbed differential growth and produced a structural abnormality.
distractorExplanations.B: Normal morphogenesis produces characteristic embryonic form; the disrupted growth and structural defect indicate an abnormal process.
distractorExplanations.C: Fate mapping labels cells and follows their destinations rather than causing or defining abnormal morphogenesis.
distractorExplanations.D: Induction is signaling from an inducing tissue to a competent responding tissue and does not by itself denote abnormal form generation.

questions.learningObjective: Connect genetic and teratogenic disruption of differential growth with dysmorphogenesis.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is dysmorphogenesis? Source answer: Dysmorphogenesis is abnormal morphogenesis: perturbation of differential growth due to genetic mutation, teratogen exposure, or both, resulting in structural birth defects.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: An inducing tissue releases a signal that reaches another tissue, but the potential responding tissue is not competent to respond. Which conclusion best follows?

options.text: Signal diffusion alone is sufficient to establish induction
The presence of an inducing tissue alone is sufficient to establish induction
Induction requires removal of the potential responding tissue
Induction requires both an inducer and a competent responder, so the interaction is incomplete

acceptedFreeText: Induction requires both an inducer and a competent responder, so the interaction is incomplete
questions.explanation: Induction requires an inducing tissue that provides a signal and a competent responding tissue whose fate or behavior can be changed. Signal delivery without responder competence is insufficient.

distractorExplanations.A: Diffusion can bring a secreted signal to responder cells, but induction also requires that those cells be competent.
distractorExplanations.B: An inducing tissue is necessary but is not sufficient without a competent responding tissue.
distractorExplanations.C: Removing tissue is ablation, an experimental test of necessity; it is not a requirement for induction.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly identifies the two required components of induction: an inducer and a competent responder.

questions.learningObjective: Identify inducer presence and responder competence as necessary components of induction.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Define induction in developmental biology. Source answer: Induction is an interaction where one tissue (inducing tissue) sends signals that change the fate or behavior of another tissue (responding tissue), often via secreted growth factors. It requires an inducer and a competent responder.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: An investigator performs three experiments: removes a tissue to test whether it is necessary, moves a tissue to a new location to test its effects, and labels cells to track their destinations. Which sequence correctly names these techniques?
questions.explanation: Removal to test necessity is cutting or ablation; movement to a new location is pasting or transplantation; labeling and tracking cells is painting or fate mapping.

distractorExplanations.A: Transplantation moves tissue rather than removing it, and fate mapping labels cells rather than moving tissue.
distractorExplanations.B: This correctly matches removal with ablation, relocation with transplantation, and cell tracking with fate mapping.
distractorExplanations.C: Fate mapping does not remove tissue, and ablation does not relocate it.
distractorExplanations.D: The first technique is correctly identified, but labeling and tracking is fate mapping, whereas moving tissue is transplantation.

questions.learningObjective: Match ablation, transplantation, and fate mapping to the experimental questions they address.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are the three classical experimental embryology techniques nicknamed 'cutting, pasting, and painting'? Source answer: • Cutting (extirpation/ablation): remove tissues to test necessity. • Pasting (transplantation/grafting): move tissues to new locations to test sufficiency/competence. • Painting (fate mapping): label cells (e.g., with dyes) and track where they end up.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts cadherins with the listed cell adhesion molecules (CAMs)?

options.text: Cadherins are Ca²⁺-dependent and mediate homophilic cell–cell adhesion; N-CAM, V-CAM, and PECAM are Ca²⁺-independent CAMs involved in cell–cell interactions
Cadherins are Ca²⁺-independent, whereas N-CAM, V-CAM, and PECAM are Ca²⁺-dependent
Both cadherins and CAMs are Ca²⁺-independent and do not mediate cell–cell interactions
N-CAM, V-CAM, and PECAM are cadherins, whereas E-cadherin, N-cadherin, and P-cadherin are CAMs of a separate Ca²⁺-independent group

acceptedFreeText: Cadherins are Ca²⁺-dependent and mediate homophilic cell–cell adhesion; N-CAM, V-CAM, and PECAM are Ca²⁺-independent CAMs involved in cell–cell interactions
questions.explanation: Cadherins, including E-, N-, and P-cadherin, are Ca²⁺-dependent molecules that mediate homophilic cell–cell adhesion. N-CAM, V-CAM, and PECAM are Ca²⁺-independent CAMs that also mediate cell–cell interactions.

distractorExplanations.A: This correctly states the calcium dependence, examples, and cell–cell adhesive roles of both groups.
distractorExplanations.B: The calcium requirements are reversed: cadherins are Ca²⁺-dependent, whereas the listed CAMs are Ca²⁺-independent.
distractorExplanations.C: Cadherins are Ca²⁺-dependent, and both groups participate in cell–cell interactions.
distractorExplanations.D: The examples are assigned to the wrong groups, and the cadherins listed are Ca²⁺-dependent.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate cadherins and CAMs by calcium dependence and representative molecules.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are cadherins and CAMs? Source answer: • Cadherins: Ca²⁺-dependent adhesion molecules (e.g., N-cadherin, E-cadherin, P-cadherin) mediating homophilic cell–cell adhesion within tissues. • CAMs (cell adhesion molecules): Ca²⁺-independent adhesion molecules (N-CAM, V-CAM, PECAM) also mediating cell–cell interactions.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which combination consists of principal components of the embryonic basement membrane?

options.text: Type IV collagen, N-CAM, V-CAM, and PECAM
Heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, Nodal, and activin
Type IV collagen, laminin, fibronectin, and perlecan
Fibronectin, interstitial collagens, heparan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate

acceptedFreeText: Type IV collagen, laminin, fibronectin, and perlecan
questions.explanation: The embryonic basement membrane is composed mainly of type IV collagen, laminin, fibronectin, and associated proteoglycans such as perlecan.

distractorExplanations.A: N-CAM, V-CAM, and PECAM are cell adhesion molecules rather than the listed principal basement-membrane components.
distractorExplanations.B: Heparan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate are interstitial extracellular-matrix proteoglycans, while Nodal and activin belong to the TGFβ superfamily.
distractorExplanations.C: This is the listed combination of principal basement-membrane components.
distractorExplanations.D: This combination describes key components of the interstitial extracellular matrix rather than the principal basement-membrane combination.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the principal molecular components of embryonic basement membrane.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are key components of the extracellular matrix and basement membrane in embryos? Source answer: • Basement membrane: mainly type IV collagen, laminin, fibronectin, and associated proteoglycans (e.g., perlecan). • Interstitial ECM: fibronectin, collagens, proteoglycans such as heparan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly traces a generic inductive signal from its production to a change in responder-cell fate?

options.text: Ligand secretion → receptor binding → diffusion through ECM → transcription-factor modulation → signal transduction → altered cell fate
Ligand secretion → diffusion through ECM → receptor binding → intracellular signal transduction → transcription-factor modulation and altered gene expression → altered cell behavior and fate
Diffusion through ECM → ligand secretion → intracellular signal transduction → receptor binding → altered cell behavior → transcription-factor modulation
Ligand secretion → altered gene expression → diffusion through ECM → receptor binding → altered cell fate → intracellular signal transduction

acceptedFreeText: Ligand secretion → diffusion through ECM → receptor binding → intracellular signal transduction → transcription-factor modulation and altered gene expression → altered cell behavior and fate
questions.explanation: Inducer cells first secrete a ligand, which diffuses through the extracellular matrix and binds specific cell-surface receptors. Intracellular signal transduction then modulates transcription factors and gene expression, changing cell behavior and ultimately cell fate.

distractorExplanations.A: Receptor binding must follow diffusion to the responder, and intracellular signal transduction precedes transcription-factor modulation.
distractorExplanations.B: This sequence correctly orders secretion, diffusion, receptor binding, signal transduction, gene-expression change, and the resulting change in behavior and fate.
distractorExplanations.C: The ligand must be secreted before it diffuses, and receptor binding precedes intracellular signal transduction.
distractorExplanations.D: Altered gene expression and cell fate are downstream outcomes, not events preceding diffusion, receptor binding, and signal transduction.

questions.learningObjective: Order the major events connecting an extracellular inductive signal to altered cell fate.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Outline the generic signaling cascade from inducer to cell fate change. Source answer: 1) Inducer cells secrete a signaling molecule (growth factor) 2) Ligand diffuses through ECM to responder cells 3) Ligand binds specific cell-surface receptor(s) 4) Intracellular signal transduction cascade activates (e.g., phosphorylation cascades) 5) Transcription factors are modulated, altering gene expression 6) Changes in cell behavior (proliferation, survival, migration, differentiation) and ultimately cell fate.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which description best identifies the vertebrate phylotypic stage?

options.text: A pattern of multiple primary malformations sharing one underlying cause
Abnormal morphogenesis caused by genetic mutation, teratogen exposure, or both
A method that profiles all mRNAs in individual embryonic cells
A mid-embryonic stage during organogenesis when vertebrate embryos strongly resemble one another and display features such as somites, pharyngeal arches, a ventral heart tube, head, eyes, and tail

acceptedFreeText: A mid-embryonic stage during organogenesis when vertebrate embryos strongly resemble one another and display features such as somites, pharyngeal arches, a ventral heart tube, head, eyes, and tail
questions.explanation: The phylotypic stage is a mid-embryonic period during organogenesis when vertebrate embryos strongly resemble one another. Somites, pharyngeal arches, a ventral heart tube, head, eyes, and tail are characteristic, and conserved patterning genes such as Hox genes are prominently expressed.

distractorExplanations.A: This describes a syndrome rather than an embryonic stage.
distractorExplanations.B: This defines dysmorphogenesis rather than the phylotypic stage.
distractorExplanations.C: This describes single-cell RNA sequencing, an investigative method rather than a developmental stage.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly states the timing, cross-vertebrate resemblance, and characteristic features of the phylotypic stage.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the timing and characteristic features of the vertebrate phylotypic stage.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is the phylotypic stage? Source answer: The phylotypic stage is a mid-embryonic stage during organogenesis when vertebrate embryos strongly resemble each other. Features: somites, pharyngeal arches, ventral heart tube, head, eyes, and tail; conserved patterning genes (e.g., Hox) are prominently expressed.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Investigators need to profile all mRNAs separately in individual embryonic cells to identify rare populations and reconstruct developmental trajectories. Which method best meets these goals?
questions.explanation: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles all mRNAs in individual cells. It can reveal cell-type diversity, rare populations, developmental trajectories, gene regulatory networks, lineage origins, and differences between species.

distractorExplanations.A: Single-cell RNA sequencing directly provides individual-cell mRNA profiles and supports identification of rare populations and developmental trajectories.
distractorExplanations.B: Ablation removes tissues to test whether they are necessary; it does not profile mRNAs in individual cells.
distractorExplanations.C: Transplantation moves tissues to new locations to test sufficiency or competence; it does not generate individual-cell transcript profiles.
distractorExplanations.D: Fate mapping labels cells and follows where they end up, but it does not profile all mRNAs in each cell.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the embryologic questions addressed by single-cell RNA sequencing.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is single-cell RNA sequencing used for in embryology? Source answer: Single-cell RNA-seq profiles all mRNAs in individual cells, revealing: • Cell type diversity and rare cell populations • Developmental trajectories and gene regulatory networks • Differences between species (e.g., mouse vs human early embryos) • Origins of specific lineages (e.g., hematopoietic stem cells, radial glia).

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which group consists entirely of members of the TGFβ superfamily?

options.text: E-cadherin, N-cadherin, P-cadherin, N-CAM, and PECAM
Type IV collagen, laminin, fibronectin, and perlecan
TGFβ1–3, BMPs, activin/inhibin, Nodal, and anti-Müllerian hormone
Fibronectin, collagens, heparan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate

acceptedFreeText: TGFβ1–3, BMPs, activin/inhibin, Nodal, and anti-Müllerian hormone
questions.explanation: The TGFβ superfamily includes TGFβ1–3, bone morphogenetic proteins, activin and inhibin, Nodal, anti-Müllerian hormone, and related ligands.

distractorExplanations.A: These are cadherins and other cell adhesion molecules, not a list of TGFβ-superfamily ligands.
distractorExplanations.B: These are principal components of the basement membrane rather than TGFβ-superfamily members.
distractorExplanations.C: Every member listed belongs to the TGFβ superfamily.
distractorExplanations.D: These are components of the interstitial extracellular matrix rather than TGFβ-superfamily members.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the major ligand families included in the TGFβ superfamily.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What families belong to the TGFβ superfamily? Source answer: • TGFβ1–3 • Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) • Activin/inhibin • Nodal • Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH/MIS) and related ligands.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which statement best integrates the central relationship among normal embryonic development, structural birth defects, and the methods used to study them?

options.text: Morphogenesis depends on a single cell behavior, and dysmorphogenesis has exclusively genetic causes

Conserved cell behaviors and signaling pathways drive morphogenesis; genetic or environmental perturbations can produce dysmorphogenesis and structural birth defects, which can be investigated using experimental models and modern technologies
Structural birth defects are exclusively mechanical deformations and cannot be investigated experimentally
Signaling pathways determine cell fate, but cell behaviors do not contribute to three-dimensional embryonic form

acceptedFreeText: Conserved cell behaviors and signaling pathways drive morphogenesis; genetic or environmental perturbations can produce dysmorphogenesis and structural birth defects, which can be investigated using experimental models and modern technologies
questions.explanation: Embryonic morphogenesis is driven by conserved cell behaviors and signaling pathways. Genetic or environmental perturbations can cause dysmorphogenesis and structural birth defects, whose mechanisms and risks can be studied using animal models, experimental embryology, and modern genomic and stem-cell technologies.

distractorExplanations.A: Morphogenesis involves multiple cell behaviors, and dysmorphogenesis can result from genetic mutation, teratogen exposure, or both.
distractorExplanations.B: This correctly integrates the mechanisms of normal morphogenesis, the origins of dysmorphogenesis, and the methods used to study developmental abnormalities.
distractorExplanations.C: Structural birth defects include malformations as well as mechanically produced deformations, and their mechanisms can be investigated experimentally.
distractorExplanations.D: Changes in cell shape, size, position, number, and adhesivity generate differential growth and therefore contribute directly to three-dimensional embryonic form.

questions.learningObjective: Integrate cell behavior, developmental signaling, dysmorphogenesis, and experimental approaches into a unified account of embryonic development.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Summarize the central concept of this chapter in one sentence. Source answer: Embryonic morphogenesis is driven by conserved cell behaviors and signaling pathways; perturbations by genes or environment produce dysmorphogenesis and structural birth defects, whose mechanisms and risks we can understand using animal models, experimental embryology, and modern genomic and stem-cell technologies.

questions.subject: embryology

questions.subject: embryology

options.text: Birth defect, congenital malformation, and congenital anomaly

questions.explanation: Birth defect, congenital malformation, and congenital anomaly are synonymous terms for structural, functional, behavioral, or metabolic disorders present at birth.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A student claims that an embryo surviving an insult during the first week cannot have a significant malformation. Which finding makes this conclusion unreliable?

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which description best meets the definition of a deformation?

options.text: An abnormal form or position produced over time by mechanical forces acting on an otherwise normal structure
A recognizable group of anomalies with a single known cause and a definable recurrence risk
The clinical study and diagnosis of congenital structural defects and patterns of malformation

distractorExplanations.A: This states the traditional all-or-none outcome while recognizing that the concept concerns insults before the third week.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Two embryos are exposed to the same developmental agent. Embryo 1 receives a lower dose for a shorter duration, whereas embryo 2 receives a higher dose for a longer duration. Which prediction best follows the dose–duration principle of teratology?

options.text: Embryo 1 generally has a greater likelihood and severity of abnormal development.
Both embryos necessarily have identical developmental outcomes.
Embryo 2 generally has a greater likelihood and severity of abnormal development.
Embryo 2 generally has a lower likelihood and severity of abnormal development.

acceptedFreeText: Embryo 2 generally has a greater likelihood and severity of abnormal development.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the principle because embryo 1 has both the lower dose and the shorter exposure.
distractorExplanations.B: The principle predicts a general increase in risk with dose and duration, not necessarily identical outcomes.
distractorExplanations.C: Embryo 2 has both the higher dose and longer exposure, which generally increase the likelihood and severity of abnormal development.

questions.prompt: An embryo has a spectrum of midline closure defects extending from the lower sternum to the upper abdomen, including ectopia cordis, an anterior diaphragmatic defect, absence of pericardium, a sternal defect, and an abdominal wall defect. Which diagnosis best encompasses this pattern?
questions.explanation: Cantrell pentalogy is a spectrum of midline closure defects from the lower sternum to the upper abdomen. Its features include ectopia cordis, an anterior diaphragmatic defect, absence of pericardium, sternal defects, and abdominal wall defects such as omphalocele and/or gastroschisis.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A patient can feel sustained pressure but cannot detect a pinprick, an excessively hot surface, or histamine-induced itching in a patch of skin. Which receptor type is most directly impaired?
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings extend through the papillary dermis into lower epidermal layers and are the principal cutaneous receptors for pain, temperature extremes, and itching. They can also contribute to crude touch.

distractorExplanations.B: Merkel complexes are tonic mechanoreceptors for sustained light touch and texture, not the principal receptors for pain, temperature, and itch.
distractorExplanations.C: Meissner corpuscles are encapsulated phasic receptors for light touch and low-frequency deformation.
distractorExplanations.D: Pacinian corpuscles are deep encapsulated receptors for coarse pressure and high-frequency vibration.

questions.learningObjective: Associate free nerve endings with pain, temperature, itching, and crude tactile input.

source.excerpt: Epidermal free nerve endings detect pain, temperature extremes, itching, and mechanical movements of the skin.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which receptor-location-function combination best identifies the tonic receptor that continues signaling while a small object presses against the skin?

options.text: Merkel cell-neurite complex in the stratum basale; sustained light touch and texture
Meissner corpuscle in the hypodermis; high-frequency vibration
Pacinian corpuscle in the epidermis; pain and temperature
Root hair plexus in glabrous skin; sustained deep pressure

acceptedFreeText: Merkel cell-neurite complex in the stratum basale; sustained light touch and texture
questions.explanation: Merkel cells lie in the basal epidermis and contact expanded sensory axon endings. Their tonic response preserves information about sustained light touch and surface texture.

distractorExplanations.B: Meissner corpuscles lie in dermal papillae and respond rapidly to light touch or low-frequency deformation.
distractorExplanations.C: Pacinian corpuscles are deep in reticular dermis or hypodermis and detect pressure and high-frequency vibration.
distractorExplanations.D: Root hair plexuses surround hair follicles in hairy skin and respond to hair movement.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology

questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are large, deeply located, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors whose concentric lamellae transmit changes in coarse pressure and high-frequency vibration to the central axon.

distractorExplanations.B: Root hair plexuses detect displacement of hairs rather than deep high-frequency vibration.
distractorExplanations.D: Free nerve endings mainly signal pain, temperature, itch, and some crude touch.

questions.prompt: A slight breeze bends hairs on the forearm without appreciably indenting the skin. Which receptor transduces this movement most directly?

distractorExplanations.B: Pacinian corpuscles respond to deeper pressure and high-frequency vibration.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A light-microscopy stain shows a basement membrane beneath an epithelium. Which statement best distinguishes it from the basal lamina?

options.text: The basement membrane includes the epithelial basal lamina plus an underlying reticular lamina
The basement membrane is only the lamina lucida, whereas the basal lamina is only the lamina densa
The basal lamina is made by fibroblasts, whereas the basement membrane is made only by epithelial cells
The terms describe two unrelated structures on opposite surfaces of an epithelial cell

questions.explanation: The basal lamina is an epithelial extracellular-matrix layer; the light-microscopic basement membrane includes it together with the connective-tissue reticular lamina.

distractorExplanations.B: Lamina lucida and lamina densa are subdivisions associated with the basal lamina, not the stated distinction.
distractorExplanations.C: The production relationship is reversed and oversimplified: epithelial cells contribute basal-lamina components, while connective-tissue cells contribute the reticular lamina.
distractorExplanations.D: Both structures are at the basal interface and are closely related.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which platelet structure–content pairing is correct?

options.text: Peripheral hyalomere: microtubule marginal bundle; alpha granules: fibrinogen and platelet-derived growth factor; dense granules: ADP and calcium
Central granulomere: hemoglobin; alpha granules: histamine only; dense granules: collagen type I
Peripheral hyalomere: nucleus and rough ER; alpha granules: DNA; dense granules: myelin basic protein
Open canalicular system: actin-free lipid droplets; alpha granules: bile salts; dense granules: thyroxine

questions.explanation: The pale peripheral hyalomere contains the cytoskeleton including the marginal microtubule bundle. The central granulomere contains alpha granules with adhesive/growth proteins and dense granules rich in ADP, ATP, calcium, and serotonin.

distractorExplanations.B: Platelets lack hemoglobin-rich granulomeres, and the granule contents are wrong.
distractorExplanations.C: Platelets are anucleate and do not store DNA or myelin protein in their granules.
distractorExplanations.D: The open canalicular system communicates with the surface and supports secretion; the listed contents are unrelated.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes neutrophil primary from secondary granules?

Primary granules contain hemoglobin; secondary granules contain immunoglobulin
Primary granules contain histamine and heparin; secondary granules contain major basic protein
Primary granules contain insulin; secondary granules contain collagen type II

questions.explanation: Primary azurophilic granules are lysosome-like and contain myeloperoxidase, acid hydrolases, and antimicrobial proteins. Secondary specific granules include lactoferrin, lysozyme, and other antimicrobial components.

distractorExplanations.C: Histamine/heparin suggest basophil or mast-cell granules; major basic protein is characteristic of eosinophils.

questions.prompt: Which tissue is shown, with chondrocytes in lacunae, isogenous groups, and a smooth basophilic matrix?

distractorExplanations.B: Elastic cartilage contains branching elastic fibers and usually a perichondrium.

questions.prompt: What structural unit is centered on the dark canal in this compact bone field?

distractorExplanations.C: An epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage organized into zones of chondrocyte maturation.
distractorExplanations.D: Perichondrium surrounds most cartilage and is not a unit of compact bone.

questions.prompt: The sequence from a two-cell embryo to a compact ball of blastomeres is which developmental process?

Neurulation ending in a neural tube

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: In the ventricular fast-response action potential shown, which ionic event produces the very steep phase labeled 0?

options.text: Rapid Na+ influx through fast voltage-gated Na+ channels
Slow Ca2+ influx through L-type channels
K+ efflux through delayed rectifier channels
Inward Na+ current through funny (If) channels

questions.explanation: Phase 0 of a ventricular or Purkinje fast-response action potential is the rapid upstroke caused by opening of fast voltage-gated Na+ channels and a large inward Na+ current.

distractorExplanations.B: L-type Ca2+ influx is central to the phase 2 plateau, not the fast phase 0 upstroke of ventricular muscle.
distractorExplanations.C: Delayed rectifier K+ currents dominate phase 3 repolarization.
distractorExplanations.D: Funny current drives spontaneous phase 4 depolarization in pacemaker cells, not ventricular phase 0.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Which combination of currents best explains the sustained phase labeled 2 in this ventricular action-potential diagram?

options.text: Inward L-type Ca2+ current balanced by outward K+ current
Funny Na+ current balanced by Cl- influx

acceptedFreeText: calcium influx balanced by potassium efflux
L-type Ca2+ in and K+ out
questions.explanation: The ventricular plateau is sustained because inward Ca2+ through slow L-type channels is approximately balanced by outward K+ current. This prolongs contraction and the refractory period.

distractorExplanations.A: Fast Na+ channels inactivate after phase 0 and cannot sustain the plateau.
distractorExplanations.C: Funny current is a pacemaker current during phase 4, and Cl- influx is not the principal plateau mechanism.
distractorExplanations.D: The Na+/K+-ATPase restores gradients over time but does not generate the plateau contour.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: The red pacemaker trace reaches threshold sooner than the gray trace. Which mechanism produces this sympathetic effect?

options.text: Beta1 receptor activation increases cAMP, enhancing If and Ca2+ currents
M2 receptor activation opens K+ channels and lowers cAMP
Fast ventricular Na+ channels remain open during phase 4
Reduced funny current makes phase 4 less steep

questions.explanation: Beta1 stimulation raises cAMP in SA-nodal cells, increasing funny current and Ca2+ channel activity. Phase 4 becomes steeper, threshold is reached earlier, and heart rate rises.

distractorExplanations.B: M2 signaling is parasympathetic and slows pacemaker firing by hyperpolarizing the cell and reducing cAMP.
distractorExplanations.C: The nodal upstroke depends mainly on Ca2+ channels; fast ventricular Na+ channels do not create the phase 4 slope.
distractorExplanations.D: Reducing If would flatten phase 4 and delay threshold rather than accelerating the rate.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: The blue pacemaker trace is hyperpolarized and has a shallower phase 4 slope. Which receptor-effector pair best explains it?

options.text: Beta1 receptor; increased adenylyl cyclase activity
M2 receptor; Gi signaling with increased K+ conductance
Alpha1 receptor; increased IP3 in ventricular muscle
Nicotinic receptor; direct opening of fast Na+ channels in the SA node

questions.explanation: ACh acting at M2 receptors activates Gi, lowers cAMP and enhances K+ conductance. The maximum diastolic potential becomes more negative and spontaneous depolarization slows.

distractorExplanations.A: Beta1 signaling raises cAMP and accelerates pacemaker firing, the opposite of the blue trace.
distractorExplanations.C: Alpha1-IP3 signaling is not the principal mechanism of vagal slowing at the SA node.
distractorExplanations.D: Autonomic ganglionic nicotinic receptors do not directly create this SA-nodal membrane response.

questions.prompt: On the red ventricular pressure-volume loop, what occurs during the vertical segment labeled II?

options.text: Ventricular filling with the mitral valve open
Isovolumic contraction with both valves closed
Ventricular ejection with the aortic valve open
Isovolumic relaxation after the mitral valve opens

questions.prompt: The QRS complex shown has nearly equal positive and negative deflections. In the equiphasic method, the mean QRS axis should be oriented how relative to this lead?

options.text: Parallel to the lead's positive axis
Exactly 180 degrees from the lead's positive axis
It cannot be estimated from an equiphasic lead

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Which anatomical position corresponds to the electrode labeled V1 in this placement diagram?

options.text: Fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border
Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
Same horizontal level as V4 at the left midaxillary line
